To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) CURB-65 and CRB-65 scores are not associated with mortality in patients with pneumonia and 2) CURB- and CRB-based scores are not useful in predicting pneumonia-related mortality in patients with community-acquired pneumonia.

the use of the pneumonia severity score CURB-65 and the pneumonia prognostic rules in primary care.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CURB65 is not a good predictor of mortality for community acquired pneumonia.

CURB-65 has been validated for use in predicting the need for hospitalisation and mortality in patients with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), but not for the need of intravenous antibiotics, and not for CAP in children.
CURB-65 has a good predictive value in the assessment of patients with community acquired pneumonia, but it is not a perfect test.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CURB-65 and qSOFA scores are not good enough to rule in pneumonia in patients with CAP, even in patients with a normal CRP level, and that the CRP and CURB-65 scores are not good at ruling out pneumonia in patients with a low CRP level.
the CURB-65 criteria can be used in a clinical setting for the assessment of pneumonia severity and to determine the most appropriate treatment, and that it has a good predictive value for mortality.
CURB-65 and qSOFA have a good predictive performance, and the combination of both scores has the best performance.
